toolUseResult.stdout:
[Title] Pirate Sea Race Game Specification [Subtitle] Game design and browser multiplayer implementation plan Version 0.1 • 23 September 2026 • Proposed baseline for playtesting Build an eight-player pirate treasure race in which players explore a shared sea, discover supernatural powers, collect four different poneglyph rubbings, and race to the final treasure. Rival pirates can interrupt that journey through short, skill-based duels and steal a missing rubbing from the loser. The strongest part of the concept is the choice between exploration and confrontation. A player can seek a remote ruin, follow a rumor, chase someone carrying a missing clue, or take a risky route to the finish. Combat matters because of what is at stake in the world. The recommended format combines a top-down overworld with side-view, single-plane fighting arenas. The match continues while two players duel. Defeat removes one objective item and some match currency, but preserves the player’s fruit, fighting kit, and remaining clues. Setting | Proposed first release Players | 8 solo players per match Session | Aim for 20–30 minutes; hard stop at 35 minutes World | 12 explorable islands plus one hidden final island Objective | Hold one rubbing of each of four distinct types Victory | Reach the treasure and complete a 10-second claim Battles | Instanced 1v1 duels; one 60-second round Platforms | Desktop browsers; keyboard first; controller support Progression | Match power resets; account rewards are cosmetic
All numerical values in this document are initial tuning parameters, not validated balance or performance results. One Piece terms describe the requested fantasy. The proposed production direction uses original characters, island names, power names, art, music, and treasure lore. Brand and licensing choices remain a separate product decision. This specification defines the playable rules, system boundaries, edge cases, implementation structure, and release gates. [Heading1] 1 The player experience [Heading2] Core loop Spawn at a fair starting location, sail toward a lead, explore an island, gain a power or rubbing, assess nearby rivals, fight or evade, and choose the next destination. Once all four types are held, the compass reveals the final treasure. The player must still travel there and defend the claim. Three decisions should repeatedly matter: where to go next, whether a fight is worth the lost time, and which abilities suit the player’s approach. Sailing should create encounters and anticipation; it must not become several minutes of empty travel. [Heading2] A representative match A player starts beside a small ship, finds a Smoke fruit on a nearby island, and reads a rumor pointing to a western ruin. Another player reaches that ruin first and leaves with the Moon rubbing. The first player can chase them or investigate a second lead. Later, the Smoke player wins a boarding duel and steals the Moon rubbing. The defeated opponent keeps their other two rubbings and Ember powers. They respawn away from the winner and pursue a different Moon source. A third player completes all four types, triggering a public rumor about the final island’s sector. The remaining players must decide whether to finish their own collection or intercept the leader. [Heading2] Design commitments [ListBullet] Exploration and fighting are both viable ways to advance. A player can win without initiating PvP, but cannot assume they will avoid it. [ListBullet] Fruit powers change play style. Finding the rarest-looking power must not automatically decide the match. [ListBullet] PvP produces a meaningful setback without erasing the loser’s whole match. [ListBullet] The destination is earned through information and inventory. Defeating the most opponents is not a substitute victory condition. [ListBullet] Every important attack has readable startup and a defensive answer available to every kit. [ListBullet] The first prototype must prove the online duel and the theft loop before adding a large content roster. [Heading2] Scope boundary The first release is a repeatable session game. Persistent shared worlds, crews, ranked seasons, elaborate naval combat, trading, sprawling quests, and mobile touch combat are later possibilities. Each would materially change balancing or production requirements. [Heading1] 2 Match rules and pacing Phase | Rule and intended effect Lobby | Public queue or private invitation code; region and connection quality shown Ready check | 20 seconds after all eight seats are filled; clients preload arenas Departure | 45 seconds of protection; players can explore and collect starter loot Exploration | All 12 initial rubbing sources are available; no time gate on collection First full set | Final-island sector announced; eligible player receives exact navigation Minute 20 | Reveal sectors containing unclaimed rubbings and abandoned rubbing caches Minute 28 | Publish approximate sectors of rubbing carriers every 30 seconds Minute 35 | Stop the match; if nobody claimed the treasure, record no winner
The match timer begins when player control starts. Eight-player public matches do not start short-handed in version one. Private tests may start with two to eight players and are marked as custom matches. Late arrivals wait in the lobby for another match; they cannot enter an ongoing race. [Heading2] Spawn fairness Select one of eight prevalidated outer-world spawn slots for each player. Randomize player assignment, island variants, and loot sockets within constraints. Give every player a ship, the same base fighting kit, 50 gold, and a rumor leading toward a reachable objective. Spawn protection permits starter loot and sailing, but collecting a rubbing or initiating a duel ends it immediately. Every slot must offer an initial useful pickup within 20–40 seconds and a plausible rubbing route within 90–150 seconds. Adjacent starting ships must not be in engagement range. These are travel-time targets to validate in playtests, not fixed guarantees based only on map distance. [Heading2] Time limits and results There is no automatic win for having the most clues at the deadline. A timeout is a draw for victory purposes; the result screen still shows exploration and duel accomplishments. If draws are common, revise travel times and information availability before adding a different scoring system. If a claim completes on the exact deadline tick, process an already-valid completed claim before the timeout. A duel still running at the deadline ends without theft. No match timer is paused for duels, loading, or individual disconnections. [Heading1] 3 The sea and islands Use a top-down tile world with a fixed navigable layout and authored island templates. Randomize their contents and approved placements. Avoid unrestricted procedural geography in the first release: travel fairness and recognizable landmarks are more valuable than unlimited map variation. Element | Initial content and behavior Sea | Connected routes, shoals as obstacles, clear docking areas Islands | 12 islands drawn from tropical, volcanic, ruin, and mist themes Final island | One of several validated hidden sockets; reachable by every ship Ruins | One globally claimable rubbing source on each regular island Other loot | Fruit pedestals, supply chests, rumor signs, and gold caches Landmarks | Visible silhouettes that help players navigate without opening a map Hazards | Clearly marked slow zones; no lethal environmental traps in version one
[Heading2] Movement and visibility Sailing uses acceleration, braking, and turning, with generous handling rather than a naval simulation. Nearby ships and islands are visible inside a defined sight radius. Unvisited territory is covered by fog on the minimap. Once discovered, terrain stays on the personal map, while enemies disappear outside current visibility. World positions are authoritative on the server. Island discovery, enemy visibility, and rumors are evaluated there. The client receives only the hidden-state information it is entitled to know. Public terrain can be shared; objective locations and the final-island choice must not be recoverable from a public random seed. [Heading2] Exploration activities Each ruin uses one of two short interactions: a three-symbol sequence or a small navigation puzzle. Reading nearby clues solves it; no external One Piece knowledge is required. Completing it permits a six-second rubbing interaction that can be interrupted by a valid encounter. Total time at a fresh ruin should be about 20–40 seconds. Rumors identify an island or sector containing a type the player lacks. Stale rumors are visibly marked after their target is claimed. The journal offers a replacement lead from remaining sources or a coarse carrier sighting. It never guarantees that the destination will remain uncontested. Target neighboring-island travel at 20–40 seconds and the longest useful crossing at 90 seconds or less. Tune map size around those times. Remove empty stretches before adding more sailing mechanics. [Heading1] 4 Poneglyph ownership and theft Poneglyphs are stationary ancient inscriptions. Players carry their physical rubbings. Use four distinct symbols: Sun, Moon, Tide, and Storm. The match contains three individually identified rubbings of each type, for 12 total. Each of the 12 regular islands begins with one sealed source; assignment is server-controlled. Rule | Exact behavior Collection | Hold interact for six uninterrupted seconds at an unlocked source Inventory | At most one rubbing of each type per player Duplicates | Cannot collect or steal a type already held; it stays with its owner Completion | Holding all four types enables final navigation and claiming Normal defeat | Winner chooses one loser-held type that the winner lacks Theft deadline | Five-second choice; default to the eligible type with fewest free sources, then fixed type order No eligible type | No rubbing transfers; the gold reward still applies Draw | Neither player loses rubbings or gold Dropping or trading | Players cannot voluntarily drop, trade, copy, or destroy rubbings
Each rubbing has exactly one location: sealed at a source, owned by a player, held in a recovery cache, or reserved inside an unresolved duel transaction. Its unique ID persists through every transfer. There is no new rubbing spawn when a player loses. [Heading2] Why multiple copies and limited theft A single global copy of each type would let one player or an abandoned session block the whole match. Three copies allow competing routes to victory. Limiting theft to one type preserves tension without turning a single mistake into a full reset. Players cannot hoard duplicates to remove every route for everyone else. This is a proposed tradeoff: the match has less total-loot brutality than an elimination game, but more opportunities for recovery and rivalry. Measure whether exploration alone is too fast before reducing the supply. [Heading2] Transfer invariants Commit a duel result and its inventory changes together, once, on the authoritative match process. A repeated result message must not repeat a transfer. Validate winner eligibility again at commit time. The 12 rubbing IDs must remain accounted for until the match ends, including when a player quits during resolution. [Heading1] 5 Finding and claiming the final treasure When a player first holds all four types, their compass reveals the final island’s exact route. The match announces that a complete set exists and reveals the island’s broad sea sector to everyone. All ships may travel there; four rubbings are required to claim the treasure, not to physically enter the island. This creates a final interception opportunity without requiring every challenger to have completed their own collection. A challenger with fewer than four can stop a leader through a duel, but cannot win until they complete their own set. [Heading2] Claim sequence [ListNumber] Reach the treasure circle while holding all four rubbing types. [ListNumber] End any protection state, stop moving, and hold interact for ten seconds. [ListNumber] Remain connected, eligible, and free of an accepted duel reservation for the entire channel. [ListNumber] On completion, the server commits the winner and freezes all match outcomes. Only one claim channel can be active at a time. A second eligible player must interrupt through a valid challenge or wait. Characters do not body-block one another in the overworld. Moving, losing eligibility, disconnecting, or entering a duel resets claim progress to zero. [Heading2] Counterplay and information Anyone in engagement range can interrupt a claim by successfully starting a duel. The claim UI shows this risk explicitly. Duels remain 1v1: surrounding players cannot damage the fighters or join halfway through. After a duel, the winner receives eight seconds to move away; objective interactions end that protection. Losing a rubbing removes claim eligibility immediately. The game cannot make a person forget a destination they have already learned; the server simply refuses an ineligible claim. Final navigation becomes inactive until the set is restored. [Heading2] Resolving simultaneous actions On each world tick, process accepted encounter reservations before advancing claim channels. If several attackers qualify in the same tick, choose the closest, then the lowest stable player ID. If several players begin claiming on the same tick, use the same distance-and-ID rule. Inputs arriving after a resolved win cannot retroactively cancel it. The ten-second channel is a deliberate addition to the original “arrive and win” idea. Test both versions. Keep the channel only if it creates exciting finishes without repeated, frustrating stalls. [Heading1] 6 Starting and leaving encounters Exploration and combat use different views, but remain parts of one live match. Each player can belong to at most one duel. Their overworld avatar becomes a non-interactive encounter marker while the duel runs, and their ship is reserved. Other players continue exploring. [Heading2] On islands A player presses the challenge action within close range and line of sight. A visible 0.6-second lunge telegraphs the attempt. The defender can move or dash out of its hit area. If it connects, the server reserves both players and starts the duel. Missing incurs a six-second challenge cooldown. [Heading2] At sea Ships use a short-range grappling action with a one-second windup and a visible aim direction. A successful grapple reserves both ships and loads the shared ship-deck arena. Escape is possible before the grapple lands. There are no cannons, sinking ships, crew stations, or separate ship health in version one. [Heading2] Reservation and transition Eligibility requires both players to be active, close enough, unprotected, and outside another duel. A reservation atomically locks their inventories. Use a three-second transition with a visible countdown; all battle assets should already be loaded. If one client fails to become ready within ten seconds, resolve that client as forfeiting. If both fail because the server is unhealthy, cancel the encounter without rewards. The dueling players enter with full duel health, fresh stamina, and the same starting Haki meter. World pursuit positioning does not grant a free opening hit. World boosts are suspended in duels and cannot expire into different combat statistics midway through a fight. [Heading2] Return to the world The winner returns to the encounter location with eight seconds of escape protection. The loser respawns after 15 seconds at a validated dock away from nearby opponents, with 20 seconds of protection. A draw returns both to separate nearby points with eight seconds of protection. Objective collection, claiming, or initiating an attack ends return protection first and is then processed normally. Keep a visible duel marker and elapsed time in the world. Live spectating is deferred to reduce stream-sniping information and avoid extra networking scope in the first build. [Heading1] 7 Fighting system The target is the satisfaction of spacing, blocking, punishing, and reading an opponent, using a single-plane 2D arena. Start with compact move lists and short combinations. A large move catalogue and complex aerial juggling would multiply animation and balance work before the core is proven. System | Starting rule Round | One round; 60-second clock; 1,000 health each Timeout | Higher remaining health wins Equal health | Ten-second overtime; then compare health again; exact tie is a draw Movement | Walk, crouch, jump, forward dash, backdash; auto-face opponent Attacks | Light, heavy, low, launcher, anti-air, throw, two kit specials Defense | Hold back to guard; down-back guards low; universal throw escape Stamina | 100 maximum; powers movement and guard integrity Haki meter | 100 maximum; starts at 25; powers armor, parry, and finisher Combos | Initial cap of five damaging hits before forced recovery
Standing guard blocks high and mid attacks. Crouching guard blocks lows, avoids highs, and loses to mids. Throws beat passive guard and have a ten-frame escape window. A universal anti-air discourages repeated jumping. Guarding costs stamina; a broken guard causes a short punishable stagger, never a full-health guaranteed combo. [Heading2] Damage and recovery Use 45 damage for a basic jab and roughly 100–150 for a committed heavy or special before scaling. Apply successive combo scaling of 100, 80, 65, 50, and 40 percent. Target ordinary successful combinations at 15–25 percent of health. The fifth damaging hit forces a non-juggleable recovery state; implement the cap in the simulation, not only in animations. Dashes cost 20 stamina; blocking a light costs 10, a heavy 25, and a special 20. Regenerate 20 per second after one second without spending or blocking. Guard break causes 30 frames of stagger and restores 30 stamina. No healing works inside a duel. Every kit must answer throws, armor, projectiles, and evasion. Both simultaneous lethal hits produce a draw. A KO on the final round tick takes priority over timeout comparison. The server evaluates both players’ hit events for the tick before declaring a KO, so processing order cannot invent a winner. [Heading1] 8 Controls and readable combat timing Action | Keyboard default | Controller default Move | WASD or arrow keys | D-pad or left stick Interact and dock | E | South face button in world Challenge or grapple | J | West face button in world Light attack | J | West face button Heavy attack | K | North face button Special one | U | South face button in duel Special two | I | East face button Dash | Shift | Right bumper Haki modifier | Space | Left bumper Throw | J and K | Light and heavy together Journal and map | Tab | View or select button
Use down plus heavy for low sweep, forward plus heavy for launcher, and down plus light for anti-air. Allow full remapping and display action names in the tutorial. Check keyboard rollover combinations. Both horizontal directions together produce neutral, independent of message order. [Heading2] Initial frame budgets Combat logic advances at 60 fixed steps per second regardless of render rate. A frame is approximately 16.7 milliseconds. Start with these shared baseline attacks; fruit-specific exceptions must be written into their data definitions. Move | Startup | Active | Recovery | On block Jab | 7 frames | 3 frames | 12 frames | Minus 2 Heavy mid | 18 frames | 4 frames | 24 frames | Minus 12 Low sweep | 20 frames | 3 frames | 26 frames | Minus 15 Projectile special | 22 frames | Projectile life | 30 frames | Spacing dependent Throw | 12 frames | 2 frames | 24 frames | Not guardable
“Minus 12” means the attacker recovers 12 frames later than the defender, creating a punish opportunity. Hitstun, blockstun, cancel windows, hurtboxes, and hitboxes live in move data and must agree with these budgets. Use a four-frame input buffer and no mandatory motion-input sequences in the first release. Show clear startup silhouettes, distinguish low attacks from mids, and provide separate feedback for guard, parry, armor, and confirmed damage. Cosmetic effects must not hide the actionable part of an attack. [Heading1] 9 Devil fruit inspired power kits Players begin fruitless with a complete Duelist kit. Eating a fruit replaces the two kit specials. Core normals, throw, guard, and universal Haki remain. All six fruit types below are first-release candidates; the first playable slice uses Ember and Smoke only. Kit | Two signature specials | Advantage | Vulnerability Duelist | Advancing thrust and counter slash | Reliable close combat and meter use | Limited long-range pressure Ember | Flame bolt and rising flare | Controls space and punishes jumps | Long recovery if attacks miss Smoke | Short feint dash and smoke screen | Changes spacing and obscures intent | Low direct damage; readable reappearance Spring | Charged lunge and rebound kick | Fast approach with varied timing | Charge can be interrupted Stone | Armored shoulder and ground burst | Wins selected close-range trades | Slow recovery; vulnerable to throws Gale | Gust projectile and retreating slash | Pushes opponents and resets distance | Weak when trapped close Beast | Pounce and claw sequence | Sustained close-range pressure | Telegraphs approach; limited reach
[Heading2] Acquisition and commitment Place 12 fruit pedestals, two of each type, across fair loot routes. They are distinct from rubbing sources. Eating takes three seconds and can be interrupted. A player may inspect the kit description before committing. After a fruit is eaten, it stays for that match; there is no fruit swapping or random reroll economy in version one. Fruit users remain viable after defeat because their fruit is retained. Fruitless Duelist remains a deliberate fighting option. Its specials must be tested against every fruit; it is not a weak starting class to escape as soon as possible. 1 [Title] Pirate Sea Race Game Specification 2 [Subtitle] Game design and browser multiplayer implementation plan 3 Version 0.1 • 23 September 2026 • Proposed baseline for playtesting 4 Build an eight-player pirate treasure race in which players explore a shared sea, discover supernatural powers, collect four different poneglyph rubbings, and race to the final treasure. Rival pirates can interrupt that journey through short, skill-based duels and steal a missing rubbing from the loser. 5 The strongest part of the concept is the choice between exploration and confrontation. A player can seek a remote ruin, follow a rumor, chase someone carrying a missing clue, or take a risky route to the finish. Combat matters because of what is at stake in the world. 6 The recommended format combines a top-down overworld with side-view, single-plane fighting arenas. The match continues while two players duel. Defeat removes one objective item and some match currency, but preserves the player’s fruit, fighting kit, and remaining clues. 7 8 Setting | Proposed first release 9 Players | 8 solo players per match 10 Session | Aim for 20–30 minutes; hard stop at 35 minutes 11 World | 12 explorable islands plus one hidden final island 12 Objective | Hold one rubbing of each of four distinct types 13 Victory | Reach the treasure and complete a 10-second claim 14 Battles | Instanced 1v1 duels; one 60-second round 15 Platforms | Desktop browsers; keyboard first; controller support 16 Progression | Match power resets; account rewards are cosmetic 17
18 All numerical values in this document are initial tuning parameters, not validated balance or performance results. One Piece terms describe the requested fantasy. The proposed production direction uses original characters, island names, power names, art, music, and treasure lore. Brand and licensing choices remain a separate product decision. 19 This specification defines the playable rules, system boundaries, edge cases, implementation structure, and release gates. 20 [Heading1] 1 The player experience 21 [Heading2] Core loop 22 Spawn at a fair starting location, sail toward a lead, explore an island, gain a power or rubbing, assess nearby rivals, fight or evade, and choose the next destination. Once all four types are held, the compass reveals the final treasure. The player must still travel there and defend the claim. 23 Three decisions should repeatedly matter: where to go next, whether a fight is worth the lost time, and which abilities suit the player’s approach. Sailing should create encounters and anticipation; it must not become several minutes of empty travel. 24 [Heading2] A representative match 25 A player starts beside a small ship, finds a Smoke fruit on a nearby island, and reads a rumor pointing to a western ruin. Another player reaches that ruin first and leaves with the Moon rubbing. The first player can chase them or investigate a second lead. 26 Later, the Smoke player wins a boarding duel and steals the Moon rubbing. The defeated opponent keeps their other two rubbings and Ember powers. They respawn away from the winner and pursue a different Moon source. A third player completes all four types, triggering a public rumor about the final island’s sector. The remaining players must decide whether to finish their own collection or intercept the leader. 27 [Heading2] Design commitments 28 [ListBullet] Exploration and fighting are both viable ways to advance. A player can win without initiating PvP, but cannot assume they will avoid it. 29 [ListBullet] Fruit powers change play style. Finding the rarest-looking power must not automatically decide the match. 30 [ListBullet] PvP produces a meaningful setback without erasing the loser’s whole match. 31 [ListBullet] The destination is earned through information and inventory. Defeating the most opponents is not a substitute victory condition. 32 [ListBullet] Every important attack has readable startup and a defensive answer available to every kit. 33 [ListBullet] The first prototype must prove the online duel and the theft loop before adding a large content roster. 34 [Heading2] Scope boundary 35 The first release is a repeatable session game. Persistent shared worlds, crews, ranked seasons, elaborate naval combat, trading, sprawling quests, and mobile touch combat are later possibilities. Each would materially change balancing or production requirements. 36 [Heading1] 2 Match rules and pacing 37 38 Phase | Rule and intended effect 39 Lobby | Public queue or private invitation code; region and connection quality shown 40 Ready check | 20 seconds after all eight seats are filled; clients preload arenas 41 Departure | 45 seconds of protection; players can explore and collect starter loot 42 Exploration | All 12 initial rubbing sources are available; no time gate on collection 43 First full set | Final-island sector announced; eligible player receives exact navigation 44 Minute 20 | Reveal sectors containing unclaimed rubbings and abandoned rubbing caches 45 Minute 28 | Publish approximate sectors of rubbing carriers every 30 seconds 46 Minute 35 | Stop the match; if nobody claimed the treasure, record no winner 47
48 The match timer begins when player control starts. Eight-player public matches do not start short-handed in version one. Private tests may start with two to eight players and are marked as custom matches. Late arrivals wait in the lobby for another match; they cannot enter an ongoing race. 49 [Heading2] Spawn fairness 50 Select one of eight prevalidated outer-world spawn slots for each player. Randomize player assignment, island variants, and loot sockets within constraints. Give every player a ship, the same base fighting kit, 50 gold, and a rumor leading toward a reachable objective. Spawn protection permits starter loot and sailing, but collecting a rubbing or initiating a duel ends it immediately. 51 Every slot must offer an initial useful pickup within 20–40 seconds and a plausible rubbing route within 90–150 seconds. Adjacent starting ships must not be in engagement range. These are travel-time targets to validate in playtests, not fixed guarantees based only on map distance. 52 [Heading2] Time limits and results 53 There is no automatic win for having the most clues at the deadline. A timeout is a draw for victory purposes; the result screen still shows exploration and duel accomplishments. If draws are common, revise travel times and information availability before adding a different scoring system. 54 If a claim completes on the exact deadline tick, process an already-valid completed claim before the timeout. A duel still running at the deadline ends without theft. No match timer is paused for duels, loading, or individual disconnections. 55 [Heading1] 3 The sea and islands 56 Use a top-down tile world with a fixed navigable layout and authored island templates. Randomize their contents and approved placements. Avoid unrestricted procedural geography in the first release: travel fairness and recognizable landmarks are more valuable than unlimited map variation. 57 58 Element | Initial content and behavior 59 Sea | Connected routes, shoals as obstacles, clear docking areas 60 Islands | 12 islands drawn from tropical, volcanic, ruin, and mist themes 61 Final island | One of several validated hidden sockets; reachable by every ship 62 Ruins | One globally claimable rubbing source on each regular island 63 Other loot | Fruit pedestals, supply chests, rumor signs, and gold caches 64 Landmarks | Visible silhouettes that help players navigate without opening a map 65 Hazards | Clearly marked slow zones; no lethal environmental traps in version one 66
67 [Heading2] Movement and visibility 68 Sailing uses acceleration, braking, and turning, with generous handling rather than a naval simulation. Nearby ships and islands are visible inside a defined sight radius. Unvisited territory is covered by fog on the minimap. Once discovered, terrain stays on the personal map, while enemies disappear outside current visibility. 69 World positions are authoritative on the server. Island discovery, enemy visibility, and rumors are evaluated there. The client receives only the hidden-state information it is entitled to know. Public terrain can be shared; objective locations and the final-island choice must not be recoverable from a public random seed. 70 [Heading2] Exploration activities 71 Each ruin uses one of two short interactions: a three-symbol sequence or a small navigation puzzle. Reading nearby clues solves it; no external One Piece knowledge is required. Completing it permits a six-second rubbing interaction that can be interrupted by a valid encounter. Total time at a fresh ruin should be about 20–40 seconds. 72 Rumors identify an island or sector containing a type the player lacks. Stale rumors are visibly marked after their target is claimed. The journal offers a replacement lead from remaining sources or a coarse carrier sighting. It never guarantees that the destination will remain uncontested. 73 Target neighboring-island travel at 20–40 seconds and the longest useful crossing at 90 seconds or less. Tune map size around those times. Remove empty stretches before adding more sailing mechanics. 74 [Heading1] 4 Poneglyph ownership and theft 75 Poneglyphs are stationary ancient inscriptions. Players carry their physical rubbings. Use four distinct symbols: Sun, Moon, Tide, and Storm. The match contains three individually identified rubbings of each type, for 12 total. Each of the 12 regular islands begins with one sealed source; assignment is server-controlled. 76 77 Rule | Exact behavior 78 Collection | Hold interact for six uninterrupted seconds at an unlocked source 79 Inventory | At most one rubbing of each type per player 80 Duplicates | Cannot collect or steal a type already held; it stays with its owner 81 Completion | Holding all four types enables final navigation and claiming 82 Normal defeat | Winner chooses one loser-held type that the winner lacks 83 Theft deadline | Five-second choice; default to the eligible type with fewest free sources, then fixed type order 84 No eligible type | No rubbing transfers; the gold reward still applies 85 Draw | Neither player loses rubbings or gold 86 Dropping or trading | Players cannot voluntarily drop, trade, copy, or destroy rubbings 87
88 Each rubbing has exactly one location: sealed at a source, owned by a player, held in a recovery cache, or reserved inside an unresolved duel transaction. Its unique ID persists through every transfer. There is no new rubbing spawn when a player loses. 89 [Heading2] Why multiple copies and limited theft 90 A single global copy of each type would let one player or an abandoned session block the whole match. Three copies allow competing routes to victory. Limiting theft to one type preserves tension without turning a single mistake into a full reset. Players cannot hoard duplicates to remove every route for everyone else. 91 This is a proposed tradeoff: the match has less total-loot brutality than an elimination game, but more opportunities for recovery and rivalry. Measure whether exploration alone is too fast before reducing the supply. 92 [Heading2] Transfer invariants 93 Commit a duel result and its inventory changes together, once, on the authoritative match process. A repeated result message must not repeat a transfer. Validate winner eligibility again at commit time. The 12 rubbing IDs must remain accounted for until the match ends, including when a player quits during resolution. 94 [Heading1] 5 Finding and claiming the final treasure 95 When a player first holds all four types, their compass reveals the final island’s exact route. The match announces that a complete set exists and reveals the island’s broad sea sector to everyone. All ships may travel there; four rubbings are required to claim the treasure, not to physically enter the island. 96 This creates a final interception opportunity without requiring every challenger to have completed their own collection. A challenger with fewer than four can stop a leader through a duel, but cannot win until they complete their own set. 97 [Heading2] Claim sequence 98 [ListNumber] Reach the treasure circle while holding all four rubbing types. 99 [ListNumber] End any protection state, stop moving, and hold interact for ten seconds. 100 [ListNumber] Remain connected, eligible, and free of an accepted duel reservation for the entire channel. 101 [ListNumber] On completion, the server commits the winner and freezes all match outcomes. 102 Only one claim channel can be active at a time. A second eligible player must interrupt through a valid challenge or wait. Characters do not body-block one another in the overworld. Moving, losing eligibility, disconnecting, or entering a duel resets claim progress to zero. 103 [Heading2] Counterplay and information 104 Anyone in engagement range can interrupt a claim by successfully starting a duel. The claim UI shows this risk explicitly. Duels remain 1v1: surrounding players cannot damage the fighters or join halfway through. After a duel, the winner receives eight seconds to move away; objective interactions end that protection. 105 Losing a rubbing removes claim eligibility immediately. The game cannot make a person forget a destination they have already learned; the server simply refuses an ineligible claim. Final navigation becomes inactive until the set is restored. 106 [Heading2] Resolving simultaneous actions 107 On each world tick, process accepted encounter reservations before advancing claim channels. If several attackers qualify in the same tick, choose the closest, then the lowest stable player ID. If several players begin claiming on the same tick, use the same distance-and-ID rule. Inputs arriving after a resolved win cannot retroactively cancel it. 108 The ten-second channel is a deliberate addition to the original “arrive and win” idea. Test both versions. Keep the channel only if it creates exciting finishes without repeated, frustrating stalls. 109 [Heading1] 6 Starting and leaving encounters 110 Exploration and combat use different views, but remain parts of one live match. Each player can belong to at most one duel. Their overworld avatar becomes a non-interactive encounter marker while the duel runs, and their ship is reserved. Other players continue exploring. 111 [Heading2] On islands 112 A player presses the challenge action within close range and line of sight. A visible 0.6-second lunge telegraphs the attempt. The defender can move or dash out of its hit area. If it connects, the server reserves both players and starts the duel. Missing incurs a six-second challenge cooldown. 113 [Heading2] At sea 114 Ships use a short-range grappling action with a one-second windup and a visible aim direction. A successful grapple reserves both ships and loads the shared ship-deck arena. Escape is possible before the grapple lands. There are no cannons, sinking ships, crew stations, or separate ship health in version one. 115 [Heading2] Reservation and transition 116 Eligibility requires both players to be active, close enough, unprotected, and outside another duel. A reservation atomically locks their inventories. Use a three-second transition with a visible countdown; all battle assets should already be loaded. If one client fails to become ready within ten seconds, resolve that client as forfeiting. If both fail because the server is unhealthy, cancel the encounter without rewards. 117 The dueling players enter with full duel health, fresh stamina, and the same starting Haki meter. World pursuit positioning does not grant a free opening hit. World boosts are suspended in duels and cannot expire into different combat statistics midway through a fight. 118 [Heading2] Return to the world 119 The winner returns to the encounter location with eight seconds of escape protection. The loser respawns after 15 seconds at a validated dock away from nearby opponents, with 20 seconds of protection. A draw returns both to separate nearby points with eight seconds of protection. Objective collection, claiming, or initiating an attack ends return protection first and is then processed normally. 120 Keep a visible duel marker and elapsed time in the world. Live spectating is deferred to reduce stream-sniping information and avoid extra networking scope in the first build. 121 [Heading1] 7 Fighting system 122 The target is the satisfaction of spacing, blocking, punishing, and reading an opponent, using a single-plane 2D arena. Start with compact move lists and short combinations. A large move catalogue and complex aerial juggling would multiply animation and balance work before the core is proven. 123 124 System | Starting rule 125 Round | One round; 60-second clock; 1,000 health each 126 Timeout | Higher remaining health wins 127 Equal health | Ten-second overtime; then compare health again; exact tie is a draw 128 Movement | Walk, crouch, jump, forward dash, backdash; auto-face opponent 129 Attacks | Light, heavy, low, launcher, anti-air, throw, two kit specials 130 Defense | Hold back to guard; down-back guards low; universal throw escape 131 Stamina | 100 maximum; powers movement and guard integrity 132 Haki meter | 100 maximum; starts at 25; powers armor, parry, and finisher 133 Combos | Initial cap of five damaging hits before forced recovery 134
135 Standing guard blocks high and mid attacks. Crouching guard blocks lows, avoids highs, and loses to mids. Throws beat passive guard and have a ten-frame escape window. A universal anti-air discourages repeated jumping. Guarding costs stamina; a broken guard causes a short punishable stagger, never a full-health guaranteed combo. 136 [Heading2] Damage and recovery 137 Use 45 damage for a basic jab and roughly 100–150 for a committed heavy or special before scaling. A frame is approximately 16.7 milliseconds. A disconnected world avatar can be challenged; if they remain absent, the ordinary forfeit rule applies. 235 If a disconnected player loses a duel, process the normal one-rubbing transfer first, move the player to their respawn state, and preserve the original seat-reservation deadline. At expiry, place their remaining rubbings in a recovery cache at that respawn dock. Do not duplicate the already-transferred rubbing. 236 A cache is placed on the nearest reachable shoreline or dock if its intended position is invalid. It never despawns during the match. Each rubbing can be collected only by a player missing that type. A six-second interaction claims one selected rubbing at a time. An empty cache disappears. 237 [Heading2] Server health versus individual connection quality 238 Individual packet loss is not a reason to cancel a losing fight. A server-detected simulation stall affecting the encounter is a separate fault. Cancel that duel without transfers, restore both pre-duel inventories, and return participants safely. Log the fault and match revision. 239 The first release stores final outcomes, not resumable live-world snapshots. A process restart cannot be described as a reconnect recovery. Add crash recovery only after the basic match and transaction model are proven. If everyone leaves, close the room and mark it abandoned with no winner. 240 [Heading1] 13 Interface art and sound 241 242 Screen | Information or action it must support 243 Landing and lobby | Play, private code, region, ping, settings, and short rules 244 Overworld HUD | Four symbol slots, compass, minimap, gold, protection timer, match clock 245 Journal | Known islands, collected types, current rumors, and power descriptions 246 Duel HUD | Two health bars, stamina, Haki, round clock, and connection indicator 247 Duel result | Winner, exact item transfer, and respawn or return countdown 248 Final race | Treasure eligibility, visible claim progress, and interruption feedback 249 Match result | Winner or timeout, route history, duels, stolen and recovered clues 250
251 [Heading2] Onboarding and accessibility 252 Offer a five-minute solo introduction: move, sail, dock, complete a ruin, guard a heavy, punish it, and understand theft. Let experienced players skip it. Provide a practice arena with an idle or scripted defensive opponent, hitbox visualization for developers, and a reset button. 253 Use shapes and names as well as colors for rubbing types. Allow larger UI, reduced screen shake, reduced flashing, separate audio sliders, and full control remapping. Supply visual equivalents for grapple warnings and claim alarms. Ensure menus work with keyboard navigation and use readable DOM text where practical. 254 [Heading2] Visual direction and production budget 255 Use a coherent original 2D anime-pirate style with strong silhouettes, bright seas, and readable island themes. Start with one shared humanoid rig or sprite base and cosmetic variations. Ship-deck and island duels share one collision layout with two backgrounds. Save unusual body proportions and bespoke movesets for later. 256 Budget roughly 18–24 shared character animation actions, plus fruit-specific effects and any required unique poses. Track walk, crouch, jump, dash, guard, hit reactions, knockdown, throw, normals, and specials in an asset manifest. A generated concept image is not a finished gameplay sprite set; animation consistency and hitbox alignment need production work. 257 Sound should communicate interaction timing: distinct cues for launch, impact, guard, parry, grapple warning, rubbing theft, and a full set. Unlock browser audio after the player’s first input. The initial client should preload shared combat assets and stream optional island decoration later. Art cannot delay the first control response by requiring the whole world to load. 258 [Heading1] 14 Browser architecture 259 Use TypeScript across the client, shared simulation, and server. Phaser supplies the 2D presentation layer. Colyseus provides authoritative rooms, matchmaking, and state synchronization. Its current documentation also describes prediction and reconciliation primitives; test the selected version against the duel requirements before committing to its APIs. [1–3] 260 261 Component | Responsibility 262 Browser client | Render world and arenas, collect inputs, predict local motion, display UI 263 Web shell | Lobby, account settings, journal UI, loading, accessibility menus 264 Match process | Own the world, visibility, inventory, timers, encounter state, and winner 265 Combat simulation | Pure fixed-step functions shared between client and server 266 HTTP service | Sessions, match allocation, profiles, and final results 267 PostgreSQL | Accounts, cosmetics, match summaries, and moderation records 268 Static hosting | Versioned client bundle, sprites, audio, and maps 269 Monitoring | Room counts, tick timings, errors, transfer audit, and latency metrics 270
271 [Heading2] Match and duel boundaries 272 Start with one authoritative Colyseus room per match. Duels are isolated simulation objects within that room, not separate servers or independent inventory owners. A match can contain at most four simultaneous 1v1 duels. Fighters receive their arena stream and permitted match announcements; other players receive only an encounter marker. 273 This removes cross-service inventory handoffs from the first implementation. The room creates a duel, freezes the participants’ objective inventories, validates the outcome, commits theft, and returns them to the world. It is the only writer for live match state. 274 [Heading2] Deployment baseline 275 For an initial private test, start with a single regional host around four vCPUs and 8 GB RAM, serving the game process behind HTTPS and secure WebSockets. Treat this as a test configuration, not a concurrent-user capacity promise. Keep static assets on a suitable static host and avoid database queries inside simulation ticks. 276 As usage grows, distribute whole matches across workers and regions. Keep each live room on its assigned process. Add shared presence or matchmaking infrastructure only when multiple workers require it. Drain existing matches during deployment instead of terminating them. Check the selected hosting platform supports long-lived WebSockets and persistent game processes. 277 [Heading1] 15 Networking for exploration and duels 278 Exploration tolerates interpolation better than a close-range fighter. Use separate update policies even though both modes share one match authority. WebSockets are a practical first browser transport, but reliable ordered delivery can stall behind lost packets; test that failure mode before promising fighting-game responsiveness. [4] 279 280 Layer | Initial engineering target 281 Render | 60 frames per second on the declared reference laptop 282 World simulation | 20 authoritative steps per second 283 World updates | Up to 10–20 updates per second, filtered by visibility 284 Duel simulation | 60 fixed steps per second 285 Duel input stream | One frame-tagged input per step, batched when needed 286 Duel corrections | Authoritative checkpoints plus accepted-input acknowledgements 287 Client history | Two seconds of serializable duel states and inputs 288 Region selection | Prefer stable round-trip latency below 100 milliseconds 289
290 [Heading2] Authoritative prediction policy 291 The server alone decides hits, health, inventories, and winners. Both duel clients run the same deterministic step function to predict their local experience. On a checkpoint mismatch, restore the authoritative state and replay unacknowledged inputs. Snapshot the complete coupled duel state, including projectiles, hitstop, timers, and random-generator state. 292 Select a shared input buffer before each duel from three to eight frames, based on the slower connection’s measured delay and jitter. Tune this policy in the spike. Late input cannot rewrite a completed server frame or committed outcome. Repeat held state for at most 250 milliseconds, then substitute neutral. Validate sequences and reject future-frame spam. 293 This is server-authoritative prediction and reconciliation. It is not a promise of peer-to-peer GGPO behavior. GGPO’s design illustrates why deterministic stepping, state restoration, and replay are important; choosing a different authority model still requires its own latency validation. [5] 294 Colyseus documents built-in prediction and rewind facilities, but the game still owns its deterministic logic and fairness policy. Do not assume generic movement reconciliation automatically produces good melee trades, throw escapes, or simultaneous hits. Prototype those interactions first. [2–3] 295 Use one 60 Hz match clock, with world logic every third step. Separate simulation from Phaser physics, render timing, particles, audio, and wall-clock calls. Replayed events use stable IDs so corrections do not play the same sound or award a pickup twice. 296 [Heading1] 16 Data contracts and security 297 298 Entity | Essential fields 299 Match | ID, rules version, private seed, phase, tick, end tick, winner ID 300 Player | Session identity, world position, mode, kit, focus, gold, protection expiry 301 Rubbing | Unique ID, type, owner kind, owner ID, revision 302 Duel | ID, two player IDs, start tick, phase, combat state, resolved result ID 303 Input | Session, sequence, simulation frame, buttons, bounded movement axes 304 Transfer | Result ID, source owner, target owner, rubbing ID, before and after revision 305 Recovery cache | ID, valid world position, rubbing IDs, creation tick 306 Result | Match ID, rules version, winner or end reason, participant summaries 307
308 [Heading2] Client intent and server decisions 309 Clients send actions such as move, interact with a target, attempt a grapple, submit combat buttons, choose a theft type, or start a claim. They never send authoritative damage amounts, owned rubbing lists, gold balances, final positions, or a declared victory. The server derives every consequence from validated intent. 310 Theft selection refers to a server-created duel result and an eligible type; it is not a general transfer endpoint. Duplicate, stale, unauthorized, or already-resolved requests return the current result without mutating state. Inventory reservations prevent the same rubbing from being collected, stolen, or abandoned twice during a transition. 311 [Heading2] Hidden information 312 Keep enemy inventories, undiscovered loot, exact carrier positions, and final-island selection out of unauthorized state payloads. A minimap overlay is not a security boundary. Use explicit per-player views and test actual network messages. Colyseus state views are a candidate mechanism for this filtering. [6] 313 [Heading2] Operational controls 314 Validate message schemas, cap message size and frequency, enforce session ownership, and use expiring reconnect credentials. A public guest can have only one active match seat per session. Guests may play private tests; stronger account controls can precede public competitive play. 315 Record input logs and authoritative event traces around disputes and errors, with a short documented retention period. Restrict administrative access and avoid logging authentication tokens. Treat match time and inventory as server data even if the browser’s JavaScript is modified. Minification is not an anti-cheat strategy. 316 [Heading1] 17 Repository and content workflow 317 Organize the project around one shared rules implementation. Keep UI and rendering dependencies out of authoritative logic so the same match can be simulated headlessly in tests. 318 319 Path | Ownership 320 apps/web | Phaser scenes, input adapters, UI shell, audio, loading 321 apps/server | HTTP endpoints, Colyseus room, sessions, persistence adapters 322 packages/simulation | Fixed-step world and duel rules; serializable state 323 packages/protocol | Message schemas, events, versions, and type definitions 324 packages/content | Fruit kits, move data, island layouts, items, and tuning 325 packages/test-tools | Headless clients, replay runner, network impairment harness 326 assets/source | Editable original sprites, animation sources, maps, and sound 327 assets/exported | Runtime atlases and optimized audio 328 docs | Rules, architecture decisions, operational notes, and asset manifest 329 infra | Container build, deployment configuration, and monitoring setup 330
331 [Heading2] Content definitions 332 Define each move with an ID, input condition, startup frames, active frames, recovery, hitbox timeline, damage, hitstun, blockstun, knockback, cancel rules, stamina cost, Haki effect, and audiovisual references. Validate references and impossible timings at build time. 333 Island templates declare spawn sockets, walkable areas, docks, interaction positions, and navigation constraints. A generation validator checks reachability and rubbing supply before a match is admitted. Author maps in a tile editor and export a documented format; avoid hardcoding every island into client scenes. 334 [Heading2] Versioning and release workflow 335 Assign a rules version and content hash to every match. The client must match the server’s protocol and required content before joining. Pin package versions after the technical spike rather than building on unbounded latest dependencies. Keep prior static client assets available while old matches drain. 336 Use automated checks for simulation invariants, schema validation, deterministic replays, and production builds. Follow with manual cross-browser playtests of animation readability, input handling, and sound. Balance data changes require repeatable combat scenarios and match playtests, not only passing unit tests. 337 [Heading1] 18 Build plan and feature boundaries 338 339 Stage | Deliverable | Exit condition 340 1 Combat spike | Two browser clients, common fighter, one arena, simulated latency | Guard, punish, throw, simultaneous hit, and reconnect cases are credible online 341 2 Complete slice | Four private players, four small islands, two rubbing types, Ember and Smoke | Explore, engage, steal, recover, and claim a treasure in one match 342 3 Eight player alpha | Four rubbing types, 12 islands, six fruits, full loss and endgame rules | Full matches complete with recoverable defeats and no lost objectives 343 4 Public beta | Onboarding, guest flow, controller support, observability, account cosmetics | Browser, network, load, and gameplay acceptance gates pass 344
345 The slice deliberately uses two types and eight rubbings, with two sources per island, to test the entire loop quickly. The final-alpha configuration restores four types and 12 sources. Keep this difference in a rules preset so slice shortcuts cannot silently ship into the main mode. 346 [Heading2] First playable content 347 One character base, one combat collision layout, two arena backgrounds, four small islands, one ship, two fruit kits, a usable Duelist kit, basic ruins, and minimal sound. Use placeholder art if necessary, but attacks still need readable anticipation and impact. 348 [Heading2] Features after the core is proven 349 Potential additions include two-player crews, bosses guarding alternative clues, stronger sea events, additional fruits, fruit awakenings, advanced practice tools, spectator support, ranked matchmaking, and mobile controls. A crew mode needs its own shared-inventory and win rules; it is not a simple lobby-size option. 350 [Heading2] People and planning assumptions 351 The critical skills are game programming, real-time networking, 2D animation, UI, sound, and playtesting. For planning, allow roughly 2–4 engineer-weeks for the combat spike, 3–5 for the complete slice, and another 6–12 for an initial alpha, with art and testing running alongside. These are rough effort ranges, not delivery commitments or validated estimates. 352 Re-estimate after the combat spike. A polished fighting game can demand much more animation and balance work than its simple 2D appearance suggests. Expanding the fruit roster before the spike passes is the most avoidable scope risk. 353 [Heading1] 19 Validation and launch gates 354 355 Area | Acceptance criterion 356 Inventory correctness | Every generated rubbing ID has exactly one valid owner; no duplicate transfers 357 Completion | Full collection, theft, recovery, and claim work across multiple simultaneous duels 358 Endgame | Claim interrupts, lost eligibility, same-tick outcomes, and deadline ordering are deterministic 359 Disconnects | Rejoin, forfeit, cache release, and quit cannot erase or duplicate rubbings 360 Hidden information | Unauthorized clients receive no secret coordinates or hidden inventory fields 361 Combat determinism | Identical starting state and input log yield identical state hashes 362 Load | Test increasing room counts with all players dueling; publish measured capacity only 363 Browser support | Current stable Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari on declared desktop test devices 364
365 [Heading2] Network and performance targets 366 Exercise 30, 80, and 150 millisecond round-trip latency; 0, 20, and 50 millisecond jitter; and 0, 1, and 3 percent packet loss. Report melee trades, throw escapes, correction frequency, and player judgments of fairness. These are test scenarios, not a claim that every combination will be acceptable. 367 Before public beta, target a p95 duel simulation step below eight milliseconds under the declared supported room load, with tick-overrun alarms. Target 60 FPS on an explicitly recorded reference laptop. Initially budget 20 MB or less of compressed assets before first play and prefetch the remaining required match content. Measure download-to-control time on a declared test connection. 368 [Heading2] Gameplay telemetry 369 Across at least 30 complete eight-player playtest matches, measure match duration, time to first useful pickup, first rubbing, first duel, average sailing gaps, abandonment after defeat, and the share of rubbings obtained through theft. Track which spawn slots and fruit kits overperform; small samples identify questions, not final proof of balance. 370 Aim for at least 80 percent of matches to produce a treasure winner before the deadline and at least 60 percent of defeated players to collect or steal another rubbing afterward. Use these as initial design hypotheses. If too few fights happen, improve encounter opportunities; if too many happen, protect time for exploration. 371 The core decision is whether players enjoy choosing between another island and another fight. If they describe sailing as waiting or combat as an arbitrary interruption, revise the transition and pacing before investing in more islands or powers. 372 [Heading1] 20 Decisions and technical references 373 [Heading2] Recommended baseline decisions 374 375 Question | Current proposal | Alternative worth testing 376 Session format | Eight-player matches | Persistent world would need a separate design 377 Loss severity | Steal one missing type | Steal all types in a separate high-stakes mode 378 Victory trigger | Ten-second treasure claim | Instant victory on valid arrival 379 Fruit selection | Find and commit during match | Draft a kit before spawning 380 Combat transition | Instanced 1v1 duels | Seamless arena bubbles after the first release 381 Travel view | Top-down sea and islands | Side-view islands only if exploration stays readable 382 Tone and branding | Original pirate setting | Licensed One Piece direction as a separate decision 383
384 The most useful next decision is the desired balance between relaxed adventure and aggressive competition. This baseline favors a competitive treasure race with time to explore. A slower adventure version should lengthen matches and deepen island activities; a faster competitive version should shorten sailing and expose more objective information. 385 [Heading2] Source notes 386 Official technical documentation was checked on 23 September 2026. The game rules, numerical budgets, stack recommendation, and milestones are proposed design choices. The sources below support framework capabilities and networking concepts; they do not establish that this game’s performance or balance targets have been achieved. 387 [1] Phaser documentation. Browser 2D rendering and framework capabilities. 388 https://docs.phaser.io/ 389 [2] Colyseus documentation. Authoritative rooms, matchmaking, and state synchronization. 390 https://docs.colyseus.io/ 391 [3] Colyseus netcode and determinism documentation. Prediction, reconciliation, and shared-step requirements. Evaluate the documented 0.18 or later APIs in the combat spike. 392 https://docs.colyseus.io/netcode 393 https://docs.colyseus.io/netcode/determinism 394 [4] MDN WebSocket reference. Browser connection API and implementation considerations. 395 https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket 396 [5] GGPO. Rollback networking, deterministic simulation, state save and restore, and speculative execution. 397 https://www.ggpo.net/ 398 [6] Colyseus State View documentation. Per-client state visibility. 399 https://docs.colyseus.io/state/view
